chapter_theme: Ainkurunuru 61 to 70, the wife's speeches of Orampokiyar's marutham: ten short retorts to a husband who goes to other women, built from the pond, the flood, the lily and the lotus, in which she mocks his new women as children and upstarts, counts the witnesses of his bathing, and turns her own body after childbirth into the ground of her refusal.

61.reading: The wife tells her husband that he is set on seeking out good women, one fine woman after another, women as rich as Kazhar of open-handed Matti, where the sweet ripe mango falls with a plop into the deep pond, and on celebrating marriage with them.
61.nuance: The doubled நல்லோர் நல்லோர் is the sting: not one new woman but a series. The falling ripe fruit belongs to Kazhar, not to the husband, so it is description of the town, not a hidden comparison; but Kuruntokai 8 opens with the same formula line, where the courtesan has the vaalai fish snatch the fruit, so a reader of the anthologies hears the fruit that drops into whatever water lies below as the man who falls to whoever is near (one pair only, a near miss on ullurai).

thinai_evidence.note: the wife's charge that he takes new wives is the marutham situation

comparisons.tenor: the good women he seeks to marry

62.reading: The wife asks her husband where his chariot now stands, having gathered up the young women of this town, while the soft-headed peahen, bright as the flowers of Indra's festival, calls in the dappled shade.
62.nuance: The simile can be read two ways: the many-coloured flowers of Indra's festival describe the peahen's plumage, or, read across the line, the gathered women of the town, bright and many as festival flowers; either way the question 'in which town now?' implies this town's women are already used up.

thinai_evidence.note: the husband's round of the town's women decides marutham despite the hill bird

comparisons.tenor: the peahen's bright plumage (or the gathered women)

63.reading: The wife tells the lord of the town where the flesh-smelling otter of the pond gets a vaalai fish for its daily food that even if her beauty wastes away she will not come near his chest, which has lain against other women.
63.nuance: She accepts the loss of her own beauty (the usual sign of a wife's suffering) as the price of refusing him, so the refusal is chosen, not forced.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife refuses the husband back from other women

64.reading: The wife tells her husband not to hide it from her: those who saw him bathing in the fine new flood with his laughing troupe, his beloved companion in his arms, were not one or two but many.

thinai_evidence.note: the husband's public bathing with another woman, the marutham charge

64.nuance: The proof is a count of witnesses, not her own sight: she argues as at law, and 'many' turns the private wrong into public talk.

65.reading: The wife tells the lord of the town of great floods, where the water-lily that sprang up in the sugarcane bed relieves the hunger of the bees, not to embrace her body, which has borne him a son, since it would spoil his chest.
65.nuance: 'It would spoil your chest' is sarcasm: his chest is kept fine for other women, and her body after childbirth is offered as the excuse. The lily that grew unplanted in a bed meant for cane and feeds the bees invites a hidden reading (the other woman, not planted in the household, feeding his appetite), but the poem never states his straying, so it fails the anchor condition and stays scene.

66.reading: The wife tells her husband that she is not quarrelling and asks him to say truly who she is, the woman who snatched away even his coming home to his rich house when he was thinking of his toddling son with his little chariot.
66.nuance: The rival has taken not only the husband but the visit owed to the child; the opening disclaimer 'I am not quarrelling' is itself the quarrel.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife asks who the other woman is

67.reading: The wife says that the woman he has just taken is a simple thing, since, they say, she sets herself against one who is no match for her and is proud of her great beauty, when those who have made the wife's bright forehead pale are more than the bees that drink the pollen of open flowers.
67.nuance: The new woman's pride is answered with a count: she is one of a crowd of rivals, so her claim to rank with the wife is the naivety the opening word மடவள் names.

68.reading: The wife asks the lord of the town where at first dawn the thick-stalked water-lily opens like the lotus whether his woman shows no regard: even while she herself holds back, the other will not hold herself in.
68.nuance: The lily that opens like the lotus is the lesser flower behaving as the greater, which is the charge against the new woman.

thinai_evidence.note: dawn and the pond flowers fix marutham

69.reading: The wife tells her husband that she has indeed seen his woman: at the great ford where many bathe, when the cool flood that came down with flowers swept away her sand-play, she stood crying till her kohl-dark eyes went red.
69.nuance: The rival is reduced to a child at play who cries over a ruined toy; the repeated line (Ainkurunuru 125) shows the jibe was a stock one.

70.reading: The wife tells the lord of the town of the great-watered, ever-yielding pond, where the heron, having eaten the many fish of the field pools, rests on the crown of the marutham tree in the field, that his women are clean and fragrant while she, who has borne a son, is like a ghoul.
70.nuance: Self-mockery as accusation: the 'ghoul' is the mother whose body has served the household. The heron that feeds on many fish and then sits clean aloft is close to an ullurai (the many fish to his many women), but a second pair is not clear, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: field pools and the marutham tree

links.note: Both open with the ripe sweet mango that falls of itself into the water below; in Kuruntokai 8 the courtesan has the vaalai fish snatch it, in Ainkurunuru 61 it drops into the deep pond of Kazhar, the town the wife uses to measure his new women.
links.teaches: Held together, the formula shows the falling fruit as the man who drops to whoever waits below, used by the courtesan to boast she caught him and by the wife to say he keeps falling into new marriages.

links.note: Akananuru 226 sets the husband's scandalous bathing with another woman at Matti's Kazhar ford; Ainkurunuru 61 makes Matti's Kazhar the standard for the women he courts.
links.teaches: For the marutham wife the patron's rich ford had become shorthand for the husband's other women, so a chief's town entered akam as a place of the hero's pleasures, not only of the patron's fame.

links.note: Both are the wife in oodal refusing the husband's chest; Ainkurunuru 63 because other women have lain on it, Kural 1311 because all women consume him with their eyes.
links.teaches: The couplet raises the bar of the older refusal: where the Sangam wife needs the touch of other women to refuse him, Valluvar's wife refuses for their looks alone, so the Kural turns a grievance about deeds into a jealousy of glances.

links.note: The same line, the otter getting a vaalai fish as its daily food, addresses the husband in both; in Kuruntokai 364 it is spoken by the household concubine answering the wife's slander, in Ainkurunuru 63 by the wife refusing him.
links.teaches: Because rival women use the identical otter line, the image belongs to the husband, a daily hunter in his own pond, and each woman fits it to her side of the quarrel.

links.note: Both have the wife charging the husband with bathing in the new flood with other women; Ainkurunuru 64 rests on the many who saw it, Akananuru 266 says the talk is loud as a feast and then that this is no grief to her compared with the oath he swore before Murugan.
links.teaches: The long poem moves the offence the short one names: in Ainkurunuru 64 the wound is that many saw, while Akananuru 266 dismisses the gossip and fixes on his broken oath, so publicity was the first charge but perjury the deeper one.

links.note: Kuruntokai 80 has the other woman announce she will bathe with lilies in her hair at the flooded ford and dare the wife to guard her husband; Ainkurunuru 64 has the wife report that many saw him bathing there with his beloved.
links.teaches: Read together, the public bathing that the wife cites as proof of his fault is the very display the rival intends as her victory, so the same act counts as scandal in one voice and as triumph in the other.

links.note: Both refuse the husband by pointing to the body of a nursing mother: Ainkurunuru 65 says her son-bearing body would spoil his chest; in Natrinai 380 the friend lists the ghee, smoke, milk and birth-smell that make them no match for the man of the courtesans' street.
links.teaches: Natrinai 380 itemises the household marks that Ainkurunuru 65 leaves as one sarcastic phrase, showing that 'it would spoil your chest' means the labour of the home set against the adorned women of the street.

links.note: In Ainkurunuru 66 the wife asks who the woman is who stole his homecoming to his toddling son; in Akananuru 16 the wife tells how a young courtesan found that son alone in the chariot street and hugged him as her own.
links.teaches: The son is the wife's claim on the husband, and the pair shows the rival reaching for it from both ends: diverting the father on his way to the child, and taking the child into her own arms.

links.note: Kuruntokai 8 has the courtesan boast that the husband talks big at her house but dances like a mirror puppet to his son's mother; Ainkurunuru 67 has the wife call the new woman naive for matching herself against her, since the women who have drawn him off outnumber bees. On one reading each woman claims the other holds no power over him.
links.teaches: Each side belittles the other through the man's nature, the courtesan by making him the wife's puppet and the wife by making him a bee of countless flowers, so neither woman's speech can be taken as the truth of the household.

links.note: Natrinai 300 has the water-lily bend to the lotus in the wind as attendants bow to an angry princess; Ainkurunuru 68 has the lily open at dawn like the lotus, while the wife complains that the other woman will not hold herself in.
links.teaches: The pairing shows that lily and lotus were a shared code of rank in marutham: in Natrinai the lesser flower bows and order holds, in Ainkurunuru it apes the greater flower, which is exactly the other woman's offence.

links.note: The line 'she stood crying till her kohl eyes went red' closes both; in 69 the river flood sweeps away the rival's sand-play at the bathing ford, in 125, a neythal poem, the clear wave snatches her doll.
links.teaches: The mockery of the rival as a crying child was a stock retort carried across landscapes by changing only the water and the toy, river flood and sand-play for marutham, sea wave and doll for neythal.

links.note: Both set the wife who has borne a son against the women he prefers: in Ainkurunuru 70 his women are clean and fragrant while she is like a ghoul; in Akananuru 26 she turns to the boy saying 'you suit the good women; I suit this rich one' after the husband shrank from her milk.
links.teaches: Akananuru 26 shows the scene behind the four-line retort, the husband's flinch from the nursing body, so the Ainkurunuru 'ghoul' reads as the wife's bitter echo of his own recoil.

source_issues: The whole decade has no colophon thurai; the speaker (the wife) is known only from the decade title கிழத்தி கூற்றுப்பத்து, so thurai_akam occasion words are left null.
66: line 1 (உடலினேன் அல்லேன் பொய்யாது உரைமோ) is not in sangamtamil.com's text; marked as our text has it.
69: line 4 repeats ainkurunuru 125 line 3 (a stock line, not an error).
